verses.text: From that first woman comes the race of women,
for from her comes the deadly race and the tribes of women,
a great trouble, living among mortal men,
sharing their plenty, but never their ruinous poverty.
Just as bees in their sheltered hives
feed the drones, partners in harmful work,
while the bees, all day until the sun goes down,
hurry about their daily work and build white honeycombs,
the drones stay inside the covered hives
and reap the fruits of others’ toil into their own bellies.
Just so, as a curse for mortal men, women
were made by Zeus, who thunders on high, to share in work
that brings pain. And he gave men another evil in place of a blessing:
a man who shuns marriage and women’s troublesome ways
and chooses never to marry reaches cruel old age
with no one to care for him. He has enough to live on
while he is alive, but when he dies, his property is divided
among distant relatives. And a man whose fate is to marry
and who gets a good wife with sound sense
finds evil competing with good throughout his life,
without a break. But a man who gets a wife of a wicked kind
lives with unending sorrow in his chest,
in his heart and spirit, and there is no cure for that misery.
So no one can deceive the mind of Zeus or escape his plans.
Even kindly Prometheus, son of Iapetus,
did not escape Zeus’s heavy anger. By force,
a mighty chain holds him fast, for all his knowledge.
When their father Uranus first grew angry with Briareus,
Cottus, and Gyges, he bound them in mighty chains,
awed by their overwhelming strength, their appearance,
and their size, and made them live beneath the wide-pathed earth.
There they dwelled beneath the ground in pain,
at the farthest edge, at the limits of the great earth,
suffering for a very long time, with deep grief in their hearts.
But Zeus, son of Cronus, and the other immortal gods,
whom lovely-haired Rhea bore through her love with Cronus,
brought them back into the light on Gaia’s advice.
For Gaia herself had told the gods everything in full:
with these brothers’ help, they would win victory and shining glory.
For a long time the two sides had fought, enduring heart-rending toil,
the Titan gods and all the children of Cronus,
facing each other in fierce battles,
the proud Titans fighting from high Mount Othrys,
and from Olympus the gods who give good things,
whom lovely-haired Rhea bore after sharing Cronus’s bed.
With heart-rending anger against each other,
they fought without a break for ten full years.
Neither side could find release or an end to the bitter struggle;
the outcome of the war hung in an even balance.
But when Zeus had given the three brothers all they needed,
nectar and ambrosia, the food the gods themselves eat,
proud courage grew in all their chests.
Once they had tasted nectar and delicious ambrosia,
Zeus, father of gods and humans, spoke to them:
“Listen to me, glorious children of Gaia and Uranus,
so I can tell you what the heart in my chest urges me to say.
For a very long time now, facing each other,
we have fought day after day for victory and power,
the Titan gods and all of us born to Cronus.
Now show your great strength and your irresistible hands
against the Titans in this grim battle.
Remember our loving kindness: after all your suffering,
you came back into the light, out of those cruel chains,
through our plans, out of the misty darkness.”

uncertainties: Verse 591 is marked for deletion in the supplied Greek. It is translated here because every assigned verse was requested.
The rare word translated as “distant relatives” in verse 607 refers to collateral heirs; their exact relationship is not specified.
In verse 619, Uranus’s response can suggest awe, admiration, or jealous resentment. “Awed” preserves the sense of being struck by their extraordinary power.
